t: Traditionally held to be records kept by Confucius's disciples, the Analects is now thought to have been compiled over about two centuries, and manuscripts of around 300 BCE show that his sayings were being gathered by the mid-Warring States period.

Its sayings teach the cultivation of ren, an all-encompassing virtue, through filial piety and li, ritual propriety, and hold that a ruler should lead by de, moral force and example, rather than by punishment.
Promoted by Zhu Xi as one of the Four Books, it was memorised with his commentary by all who sought office in China until 1905, and its ideas still influence East Asian thought and values.
dyk: Of the sayings of Confucius quoted by his second-generation student Mencius, 75% are not found in the received text of the Analects.
ev: Confucius dies; by tradition his disciples then collect and jointly edit their records of his conversations
The bamboo manuscripts now called Zhongni Said and Kongzi Said record sayings of Confucius in a format like that of the Analects
In the reign of Emperor Jing of Han an Old Text version is found hidden in a wall of the house believed to have been Confucius's
The Dingzhou and Pyongyang Analects, two handwritten copies later found in tombs, are written in the Western Han dynasty
He Yan's Collected Explanations of the Analects is written, for nearly 1,000 years the standard guide to the text
Zhu Xi promotes the Analects as one of the Four Books and writes the commentary that later displaces He Yan's
The Ming state endorses Zhu Xi's commentary on the Analects
The Qi version, lost for about 1,800 years, is found in the tomb of the Marquis of Haihun

f.made: Sayings attributed to Confucius, who died in 479 BCE, and his contemporaries, traditionally believed to have been compiled by his followers; many scholars now think it was compiled over about two hundred years in the Warring States period, reaching its final form in the mid-Han dynasty.
f.form: A classical Chinese text, the Lunyu (“edited conversations” or “selected speeches”), in twenty chapters of short passages, many opening with ziyue, “The Master said”, grouped by theme but without a continuous stream of thought.
f.where: The received text descends from Zhang Yu's composite Zhang Hou Lun; early copies include the Stone Classics of the Xinping Era at Luoyang (c. 175 CE), the Dingzhou and Pyongyang Analects (c. 50 BCE), the Haihunhou Analects and Warring States bamboo strips acquired by Anhui University.
f.known: ren, an all-encompassing virtue; li, ritual propriety; filial piety; de, a ruler's moral force; the rectification of names; “Do not do to others what you would not like done to yourself”; one of the Four Books
